title: Cleaning Products
fit_question: What is the biggest challenge you faced at your last job? What is your leadership style, and when did you use it effectively?
prompt: A prominent household-cleaning-products manufacturer believes it has an opportunity to do better in the market. What should you first ask the client?

clarifying_info.answer: Last-year revenue was $3B; the later target is a 1% revenue increase.
Dishwashing powder, clothes detergent powder, hand-wash liquid, shower gel and all-purpose soap.
No cost-saving or new-product opportunities exist.

interviewer_notes: Short interviewer-led case testing interpretation and creativity. First clarify what 'doing better' means, then focus on revenue and Exhibit 1. Strong candidates anticipate the calculation and discuss broader risks.

suggested_framework.summary: Book internal/external framework focused on revenue growth.

children.label: Price, volume, product and channel mix

stages.interviewer_asks: What does doing better mean, and how would you structure the problem?
stages.expected_answer: Clarify whether the goal is growth, share or profit; then assess price, volume, mix and channels, costs, market, competition and customers. With costs and products fixed, growth must come from price or volume.

stages.interviewer_asks: Should the client implement all proposed price changes if it wants at least 1% revenue growth?
stages.info_to_release: Current revenue $3B. Product revenue shares and volume-neutral price changes: dishwashing powder 5%/-2%; clothes detergent 20%/+1%; hand wash 30%/0%; shower gel 30%/+2%; all-purpose soap 15%/+4%. All changes occur together or none do.
stages.expected_answer: Weighted revenue change is 5%×-2% +20%×1% +30%×0% +30%×2% +15%×4%=1.3%. Revenue rises by $39M to $3.039B, exceeding the $30M target, so implement.
good_answer_signals: Weights price changes by revenue mix

stages.interviewer_asks: What should the client watch out for?
stages.expected_answer: Research may not represent every geography or demographic; communication costs may erode profit; this is a one-time lift; competitors may cut prices; antitrust may matter; and a different price combination could be better.
Pilot all changes: they add $39M or 1.3% with unchanged volume, above the 1% goal. Validate elasticity locally, monitor competitors and costs, then explore online channels and share growth.

exhibits.title: Price Elasticity
exhibits.description: Candidate-facing volume-neutral price changes and current revenue mix by product.
exhibits.key_insight: Positive weighted changes more than offset the dishwashing price cut.

math.question: What is the combined revenue impact?
givens: Revenue shares and price changes from Exhibit 1

synthesis: Implement the price package through a pilot. It increases revenue by $39M to $3.039B, a 1.3% lift above the 1% goal, with research indicating no volume loss. Validate elasticity across markets and monitor competitor response, communication costs and antitrust exposure.
common_pitfalls: Changes only favorable products despite the all-or-none condition
Calls a one-time price lift recurring growth

extraction.notes: Candidate-facing Exhibit 1 is page 97; calculated totals appear only in math. Reviewed and accepted by Claude 2026-09-30.
